name: part-policy
class: center, middle, inverse

# Part 1: What is being scored

---

# The tax, in one line

.pull-left[
**Proposition 40** (the Billionaire Tax Act):

- a **one-time** 5% tax on net worth
- on California residents on **1 January 2026**
- paid 1% a year over **five years**
- wealth valued on 31 December 2026

Directly held real estate is excluded; business real estate is not.
]

.pull-right[
**Two documents make the BSZ side's case**

1. Boll, Saez and Zucman (**BSZ**), NBER WP 35218, August 2026, with a public Excel
   workbook. Table 5, row 1: **$`r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])` billion.**
2. Galle, Gamage, Saez and Shanske (**GGSS**), expert report, 20 July 2026:
   **$100 billion**.

.highlight-box[
GGSS p.4: "a scoring of $104 billion that we round to $100 billion for simplicity."
**The two are one computation.**
]
]

---
name: part-steps
class: center, middle, inverse

# Part 2: Five steps to $`r round(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])` billion

---

# Step 1 and 2: the base, and what escapes it

**Step 1.** Forbes' real-time list on 1 July 2026: $n_0$ = `r n0` California billionaires
holding $W_0$ = $`r bn(W0, 0)` billion. **Data**, read off Forbes that day.

**Step 2.** Some wealth escapes: under-valued, hidden, or moved out in time. The authors
assume a share $\alpha$ = 10% of all of it together:

$$W^{\text{tax}} = (1-\alpha)\,W_0 = 0.9 \times `r bn(W0, 0)` = `r bn(t5$taxable_wealth[1])`$$

.highlight-box[
The 10% is <span class="guess">guesswork</span>. GGSS argue it is small: most of the wealth is
listed stock, easy to value, and 250 taxpayers can each be audited. Nobody has measured it,
because the tax has never existed.
]

.small[Details: [report, step 2](../repro.html#step-2-avoidance-and-evasion).]

---

# Step 3: the revenue

$$T = \tau \, W^{\text{tax}} = 0.05 \times `r bn(t5$taxable_wealth[1])` = `r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])`$$

That is the whole headline: **$`r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])` billion, once**, paid in five
yearly installments of about $`r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1] / 5)` billion.

```{r fig-waterfall, fig.height=3.2}
d <- data.frame(
  step = factor(c("5% of the list", "less 10% avoidance", "revenue"),
                levels = c("5% of the list", "less 10% avoidance", "revenue")),
  value = c(0.05 * W0, -(0.05 * W0 - t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1]), t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1]))
d$start <- c(0, 0.05 * W0, 0); d$end <- d$start + d$value
ggplot(d, aes(x = step, xmin = as.numeric(step) - 0.35, xmax = as.numeric(step) + 0.35,
              ymin = start, ymax = end, fill = step)) +
  geom_rect() +
  geom_text(aes(y = pmax(start, end), label = paste0("$", bn(abs(value)), "B")), vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#9aa6b2", "#e65100", "#1f6fce"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "$ billion")
```

---
name: steps-4-5

# Step 4 and 5: two income tax effects

**Step 4. Selling assets to pay raises income tax.** If a share $s$ = 1/3 of the tax is paid
by selling, and $g$ = 80% of a sale is taxable gain, taxed at the top California rate on
gains $t_{cg}$ = 13.3%:

$$E = s \cdot g \cdot t_{cg} \cdot T = \tfrac13 \times 0.8 \times 0.133 \times `r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])` = `r bn(t5$extra_ca_inctax_sales[1], 2)`$$

**Step 5. Leavers stop paying income tax.** Half the avoidance, *m* = 50%, is people leaving,
so 5% of the $`r bn(C, 2)` billion billionaires pay each year is lost:

$$L = \alpha \, m \, C = 0.10 \times 0.5 \times `r bn(C, 2)` = `r bn(-t5$annual_ca_inctax_loss[1], 3)` \text{ per year}$$

.highlight-box[
$L$ is **per year**, and Table 5 does not say for how many years. BSZ argue about 5; the
RJKDC side (Rauh, Jaros, Kearney, Doran and Cosso, who oppose the measure) counts it forever. That horizon is the biggest dispute between the sides.
]

---
name: part-rows
class: center, middle, inverse

# Part 3: The other rows

---
name: row-2

# Row 2: the billionaires Forbes misses

Above $4.5 billion, Forbes' list looks like a Pareto distribution. Below it, the list thins
out far faster than the pattern predicts, which is what missing small fortunes look like.

Filling the gap adds **`r bn(100 * (t5$n_billionaires[2] / n0 - 1), 0)`%** more billionaires
but only **`r bn(100 * (t5$wealth[2] / W0 - 1))`%** more wealth. Taxing them at a higher
20% avoidance rate gives:

.pull-left[
| Row | Revenue, $B |
|---|---:|
| 1. Benchmark | `r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])` |
| 2. + missing billionaires | `r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[2])` |
]

.pull-right[
.small[The Pareto coefficient is **research** (estimated from the data), so counting these
people is a research-based switch; the 20% is <span class="guess">guesswork</span>.
[Report, row 2](../repro.html#row-2-adding-the-billionaires-forbes-misses).]
]

---

# Row 3: who may have left

.pull-left[
```{r leavers-tab}
x <- lv
x$name <- tools::toTitleCase(x$name)
x$timing <- ifelse(grepl("^pre", x$timing), "before 1 Jan", "later")
x$wealth <- bn(x$wealth)
x$annual_inctax_loss <- bn(x$annual_inctax_loss, 3)
names(x) <- c("Person", "Left", "Wealth $B", "Inc. tax lost $B/yr")
knitr::kable(x, format = "html", align = "llrr")
```
]

.pull-right[
Assume the four who left **before** 1 January escape the tax, and three more leave later.
Revenue falls to **$`r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[3])` billion**; the yearly income tax loss
rises to **$`r bn(-t5$annual_ca_inctax_loss[3], 2)` billion**.

.highlight-box[
Why so little income tax? SEC filings show the top three pay very little state income tax
relative to their wealth: they rarely sell. Whether any of them has **legally** left is a
<span class="guess">legal judgment</span>, not data.
]
]

---
name: part-guess
class: center, middle, inverse

# Part 4: What is guesswork

---

# Every input, by origin

```{r origins, fig.height=3.6}
lev <- c("data", "research", "guesswork", "scenario", "derived", "convention")
cnt <- as.data.frame(table(factor(ins$origin, levels = lev)))
ggplot(cnt, aes(x = Var1, y = Freq, fill = Var1 == "guesswork")) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) + geom_text(aes(label = Freq), vjust = -0.3, size = 5) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#9aa6b2", "#e65100"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "inputs", title = paste(nrow(ins), "inputs of the one-time scoring"))
```

.small[The `r sum(ins$origin == "guesswork")` guesswork inputs are exactly the dials of the
[explorer](../explorer/). Full table with sources:
[report](../repro.html#every-input-by-origin).]

---

# How far does each guess move the revenue?

```{r tornado, fig.height=3.8}
keys <- c(avoidance = "Avoidance and evasion", mobility_share = "Share that is leaving",
          avoidance_small = "Avoidance, less visible", sell_share = "Share paid by selling",
          pareto = "Count missing billionaires", leavers = "Aggressive leavers")
base <- grd[row1, ]
rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(keys), function(k) {
  keep <- Reduce(`&`, lapply(setdiff(names(keys), k), function(o) abs(grd[[o]] - base[[o]]) < 1e-9))
  data.frame(input = keys[[k]], lo = min(grd$wealth_tax_revenue[keep]),
             hi = max(grd$wealth_tax_revenue[keep]))
}))
rows$input <- factor(rows$input, levels = rows$input[order(rows$hi - rows$lo)])
guess <- c("Avoidance and evasion", "Share that is leaving", "Avoidance, less visible",
           "Share paid by selling", "Aggressive leavers")   # origin labels: data/inputs.csv
movers <- as.character(rows$input[rows$hi - rows$lo > 1e-9 & rows$input %in% guess])
ggplot(rows, aes(y = input)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lo, xend = hi, yend = input), linewidth = 7, colour = "#1f6fce") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = base$wealth_tax_revenue, colour = "#e65100") +
  labs(x = "one-time revenue, $ billion (others at row 1)", y = NULL)
```

.small[Orange line: the preferred $`r bn(base$wealth_tax_revenue)` billion. Of the five
guesses, only `r length(movers)` move it on their own: `r tolower(paste(movers, collapse = " and "))`.
Counting the missing billionaires is research, and only raises it.]

---
name: part-repro
class: center, middle, inverse

# Part 5: What reproduces

---
name: repro-checks

# Checked, found, and not checked

.pull-left[
**Checked.** `r sum(tst$passed)` test expectations pass, `r sum(tst$failed)` fail
(`r tst$vintage[1]` workbook, run `r tst$run_date[1]`). They compare every formula cell the
pipeline re-derives against the workbook's own cached value, and pin the explorer to
Table 5.

**Found.**
- a block of 4 rows pasted twice in the workbook's billionaire list (244 counted, 240 real)
- Table 5 row 4 skips a deduction row 2 applies
- 9 layout and formula changes between the May and August workbooks
]

.pull-right[
**Not checked.**
- the raw inputs: Forbes wealth, tax statistics, SEC filings are taken as the workbook
  records them
- GGSS has no workbook; its $100 billion is BSZ row 1, rounded

.blue-box[
The reproduction shows the arithmetic from the authors' inputs to their tables is what the
paper says. It cannot show the inputs are right, and it cannot settle the guesses.
]

.small[[Materials page](../materials.html) &middot; [report, what reproduces](../repro.html#what-reproduces)]
]
